                                  11   this chapter.” Id. at (b)(1). Edwards held that “Section 16600 is unambiguous, and if the

                                  22   further reasoned that “[t]he restriction presumably was sought by plaintiffs in order to maintain a

                                  14            Before the Court is Defendant World Financial Group Insurance Agency, LLC’s (“WFG”

                                  15   or “WFGIA”) motion to dismiss Plaintiff Global Financial Impact’s (“GFI”) second amended

                                  16   complaint (ECF No. 81 (“SAC”)). Motion to Dismiss (“Mot.” or “Motion”), ECF No. 94.

                                  17            For the reasons set forth below, the Court GRANTS WFG’s Motion.

                                  18   I.       BACKGROUND
                                  19            The Court has outlined the factual background of this matter (and the related cases) in

                                  20   several orders, including in its order granting WFG’s motion to dismiss GFI’s original complaint.

                                  21   See Order Granting WFG’s Motion to Dismiss (“MTD Order”), ECF No. 57. Broadly speaking,

                                  22   this case involves claims by Sandra Olson and her company, GFI, against WFG for WFG’s

                                  23   alleged anti-competitive actions. Both companies are involved in selling life insurance and

                                  24   financial products. SAC ¶¶ 9, 38–39. After leaving WFG, Ms. Olson and her husband, Eric

                                  25   Olson, started their own competing business, GFI. Id. ¶¶ 38–39. Ms. Olson and GFI allege that

                                  26   WFG has suppressed their ability to compete, including by threatening personnel, interfering with

                                  27   GFI’s contracts, and more generally, inhibiting GFI’s ability to recruit agents from WFG. See,

                                  28   Case No.: 24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO DISMISS
                                                                                         1
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD            Document 141         Filed 11/04/24       Page 2 of 9




                                   1   e.g., id. ¶ 40. WFG denies the allegations and has separately brought claims against the Olsons

                                   2   and GFI. See World Fin. Grp. Ins. Agency, LLC v. Olson et al, No. 24-cv-00480-EJD (N.D. Cal.),

                                   3   ECF No. 1.

                                   4           In the Court’s MTD Order, the Court dismissed GFI’s claim for tortious interference with

                                   5   prospective economic advantage for failure to state a claim and GFI’s claim for violation of UCL

                                   6   for lack of standing. Ms. Olson and GFI filed an amended complaint, and GFI now asserts two

                                   7   claims against WFG: violation of California’s Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”), Cal. Bus. & Prof

                                   8   Code §§ 17200 et seq. and tortious interference with contract. SAC ¶¶ 112–122; 127–134. WFG

                                   9   has moved to dismiss both claims against it brought by GFI. See generally Mot.

                                  10   II.     LEGAL STANDARD
                                  11           Rule 8(a)(2) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure requires a complaint to include “a

                                  12   short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.” A complaint
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   that fails to meet this standard may be dismissed pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6). Rule 8(a) requires a

                                  14   plaintiff to plead “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.” Bell Atl.

                                  15   Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007). “A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff

                                  16   pleads factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is

                                  17   liable for the misconduct alleged.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). While plaintiffs

                                  18   must allege “more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has acted unlawfully,” the plausibility

                                  19   standard “is not akin to a probability requirement.” Id.

                                  20           For purposes of ruling on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the Court generally “accept[s] factual

                                  21   allegations in the complaint as true and construe[s] the pleadings in the light most favorable to the

                                  22   nonmoving party.” Manzarek v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co., 519 F.3d 1025, 1031 (9th Cir.

                                  23   2008). The Court need not, however, “assume the truth of legal conclusions merely because they

                                  24   are cast in the form of factual allegations.” Fayer v. Vaughn, 649 F.3d 1061, 1064 (9th Cir. 2011)

                                  25   (per curiam). Mere “conclusory allegations of law and unwarranted inferences are insufficient to

                                  26   defeat a motion to dismiss.” Adams v. Johnson, 355 F.3d 1179, 1183 (9th Cir. 2004). The Court

                                  27   may also “look beyond the plaintiff’s complaint to matters of public record” without converting

                                  28   Case No.: 24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO DISMISS
                                                                                           2
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD           Document 141          Filed 11/04/24      Page 3 of 9




                                   1   the Rule 12(b)(6) motion into a motion for summary judgment. Shaw v. Hahn, 56 F.3d 1128,

                                   2   1129 (9th Cir. 1995).

                                   3           To contest a plaintiff’s showing of subject matter jurisdiction, a defendant may file a Rule

                                   4   12(b)(1) motion. Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(1). A defendant may challenge jurisdiction “facially” by

                                   5   arguing the complaint “on its face” lacks jurisdiction or “factually” by presenting extrinsic

                                   6   evidence demonstrating the lack of jurisdiction on the facts of the case. Wolfe v. Strankman, 392

                                   7   F.3d 358, 362 (9th Cir. 2004); Safe Air for Everyone v. Meyer, 373 F.3d 1035, 1039 (9th Cir.

                                   8   2004). “In a facial attack, the challenger asserts that the allegations contained in a complaint are

                                   9   insufficient on their face to invoke federal jurisdiction. By contrast, in a factual attack, the

                                  10   challenger disputes the truth of the allegations that, by themselves, would otherwise invoke federal

                                  11   jurisdiction.” Safe Air for Everyone, 373 F.3d at 1039.

                                  12           In resolving a factual attack on jurisdiction, the Court may review evidence beyond the
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   complaint without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment. Id.

                                  14   (citing Savage v. Glendale Union High Sch., Dist. No. 205, Maricopa Cty., 343 F.3d 1036, 1039

                                  15   n.2 (9th Cir. 2003)). While the Court may consider evidence outside of the pleadings to resolve a

                                  16   “factual” Rule 12(b)(1) motion, “a [j]urisdictional finding of genuinely disputed facts is

                                  17   inappropriate when the jurisdictional issue and substantive issues are so intertwined that the

                                  18   question of jurisdiction is dependent on the resolution of factual issues going to the merits of an

                                  19   action.” Safe Air for Everyone, 373 F.3d at 1039 n.3 (citing Sun Valley Gasoline, Inc. v. Ernst

                                  20   Enters., Inc., 711 F.2d 138, 140 (9th Cir. 1983)) (internal quotation marks omitted).

                                  21   III.    DISCUSSION
                                  22           WFG moves to dismiss GFI’s two claims. The Court addresses each below.

                                  23           A.      UCL
                                  24           WFG argues GFI’s UCL claim should be dismissed because GFI lacks standing to pursue

                                  25   the injunctive relief it requests, and even if it did have standing, GFI fails to state a claim under

                                  26   any of the three UCL prongs.

                                  27           First, as to standing, the Court previously held that GFI lacked standing to bring its UCL

                                  28   Case No.: 24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO DISMISS
                                                                                           3
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD          Document 141        Filed 11/04/24      Page 4 of 9




                                   1   claim to the extent that claim was “based solely on WFG’s agreements with third parties.”

                                   2   MTD Order 11–12. The Court indicated that GFI “may have standing” to bring a UCL claim if

                                   3   that claim was based on its allegation that WFG is “making wrongful threats against WFG agents

                                   4   who join GFI and/or then try to solicit other agents after becoming affiliated with GFI.” Id. at 12.

                                   5   As the Court explained, that allegation could be separate from, and not based on, the contracts

                                   6   between WFG and its agents. Id. GFI has since clarified its UCL claim. GFI now alleges its own

                                   7   employees “have expressed concerns and fear of facing retaliation from WFG if they

                                   8   communicate with or attempt to recruit any current or former WFG agents” (SAC ¶ 60), and WFG

                                   9   has “threatened to terminate (and in many cases terminated) the spouse of any agent that moves to

                                  10   GFI” (id. ¶ 57). These allegations are separate from, and not based on, contracts between WFG

                                  11   and its agents. GFI has thus established it has standing to pursue its UCL claim.

                                  12          Next, WFG contends that GFI’s UCL claim must nonetheless be dismissed for failure to
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   state a claim. The UCL provides a cause of action for business practices that are (1) unlawful,

                                  14   (2) unfair, or (3) fraudulent. Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200. GFI asserts WFG’s conduct is both

                                  15   unlawful and unfair under the UCL.

                                  16          Unlawful prong. Both parties acknowledge that “[v]irtually any state, federal or local law

                                  17   can serve as the predicate for an action under” the “unlawful” prong of the UCL.” People ex rel.

                                  18   Bill Lockyer v. Fremont Life Ins. Co., 104 Cal. App. 4th 508, 515 (Cal. Ct. App. 2002). GFI

                                  19   identifies the following conduct it contends is sufficient to state a UCL claim: (1) WFG interfered

                                  20   with GFI’s relationships; (2) WFG conspired to and unlawfully obtained unauthorized access to

                                  21   Mr. Olson’s email; (3) WFG wrongfully terminated spouses of former WFG agents; (4) WFG

                                  22   endorsed the filing of baseless nuisance suits; and (5) WFG used its Restrictive Covenant to

                                  23   prevent GFI from recruiting WFG workers. See Opp. 10–12. The Court rejects GFI’s first

                                  24   category of conduct because “a UCL violation brought under the ‘unlawful’ prong may not be

                                  25   predicated on common law violations alone.” Gill v. Marsh USA, Inc., No. 24-cv-02366-RS, 2024

                                  26   WL 3463351, at *6 (N.D. Cal. July 18, 2024) (citing Foundry IV Inc. v. Hard Carry Gaming Inc.,

                                  27   No. CV 23-2690-KK-MARx, 2024 WL 211010 at *6–7 (C. D. Cal. Jan. 3, 2024) (collecting

                                  28   Case No.: 24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO DISMISS
                                                                                        4
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD          Document 141         Filed 11/04/24      Page 5 of 9




                                   1   cases)). Regarding the second category of alleged unlawful conduct, GFI argues that “WFG

                                   2   conspired to and did unlawfully obtain unauthorized access to Mr. Olson’s email” but fails to cite

                                   3   any supporting allegations in the SAC. Opp. 10–11. Assuming GFI is referring to paragraph 78,

                                   4   that paragraph alleges that WFG “ask[ed] the Olsons’ former personal assistant, Darren Perez, to

                                   5   obtain information” from the Olsons’ email accounts without authorization. SAC ¶ 78. WFG

                                   6   argues this cannot form the basis of GFI’s UCL claim because the SAC alleges that independent

                                   7   contractors, not WFG, engaged in this activity. That is, the SAC does not allege WFG

                                   8   “controlled, demanded or otherwise directed the alleged conduct of these individual agents.”

                                   9   Mot. 8. But paragraph 78 explicitly alleges that WFG “ask[ed]” Mr. Perez to access the Olsons’

                                  10   email account without authorization. See Bottoni v. Sallie Mae, Inc, 2011 WL 2293226, at *7

                                  11   (N.D. Cal. Jun 8, 2011) (UCL claim survived motion to dismiss where complaint alleged that

                                  12   Sallie Mae “controls” the debt collectors and “directs” the debt collectors to demand and collect
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   the allegedly illegal collection penalties). Thus, GFI has plausibly alleged WFG personally

                                  14   participated in Mr. Perez’s actions regarding the unauthorized email access. WFG’s cited cases on

                                  15   this point are therefore unpersuasive. See Opp. 8–9 (citing Emery v. Visa Int’l Serv. Ass’n, 95

                                  16   Cal.App.4th 952, 960 (Ct. App. 2002); People v. Toomey, 157 Cal.App.3d 1, 14 (Ct. App. 1984)

                                  17   (liability under the UCL “must be predicated on [the defendant’s] personal participation in the

                                  18   unlawful practices,” and not some form of vicarious liability); Friedman v. Mercedes Benz USA

                                  19   LLC, No. CV 12-7204, 2013 WL 8336127 at *6 (C.D. Cal. June 12, 2013)).

                                  20          Still, GFI’s UCL claim based on the unlawful prong fails for a separate reason. GFI has

                                  21   not identified any law––federal, state, or local––that serves as the predicate for its claim. The

                                  22   Court presumes that obtaining unauthorized access to email could violate some law, but the Court

                                  23   cannot assess the sufficiency of GFI’s claims without more information regarding which law (or

                                  24   laws) GFI claims was (or were) violated. Pinnacle Ventures LLC v. Bertelsmann Educ. Servs.

                                  25   LLC, No. 18-CV-03412-BLF, 2020 WL 1082764, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 6, 2020) (dismissing UCL

                                  26   claim because “[defendant] has not pled facts showing a violation of law by [plaintiff]”). GFI’s

                                  27   third (WFG wrongfully terminated spouses of former WFG agents) and fourth (WFG endorsed the

                                  28   Case No.: 24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO DISMISS
                                                                                         5
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD           Document 141          Filed 11/04/24      Page 6 of 9




                                   1   filing of baseless nuisance suits) categories of conduct fail for the same reason. GFI must identify

                                   2   which law it contends this conduct violates. Finally, as to the fifth category of conduct, GFI

                                   3   alleges that WFG “is using its illegal Restrictive Covenant to prevent GFI from recruiting WFG

                                   4   workers” and “to intimidate WFG workers from wanting to leave.” Opp. 11. In support, GFI does

                                   5   identify a law: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600. Opp. 13. However, these allegations are based

                                   6   on provisions in the agent agreements to which GFI is not party. As the Court previously held,

                                   7   GFI lacks standing to pursue a UCL claim based solely on the Restrictive Covenant in agreements

                                   8   between agents and WFG. See MTD Order 11–12.

                                   9            Accordingly, GFI has failed to state a claim for violation of the UCL based on the unlawful

                                  10   prong.

                                  11            Unfair prong. A competitor’s conduct or practice is unfair when it “threatens an incipient

                                  12   violation of an antitrust law, or violates the policy or spirit of one of those laws because its effects
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   are comparable to or the same as a violation of the law, or otherwise significantly threatens or

                                  14   harms competition.” Diva Limousine, Ltd. v. Uber Techs., Inc., 392 F. Supp. 3d 1074, 1090 (N.D.

                                  15   Cal. 2019) (quoting Cel-Tech Commc’ns, Inc. v. Los Angeles Cellular Tel. Co., 20 Cal. 4th 163,

                                  16   186–87 (1999)). A practice “may be deemed unfair even if not specifically proscribed by some

                                  17   other law.” Cal. Med. Assn. v. Aetna Health of Cal. Inc., 14 Cal. 5th 1075, 1085 (2023).

                                  18            GFI alleges that the same conduct identified above––stealing confidential information,

                                  19   terminating employees, and threatening the Restrictive Covenant––“significantly threatens or

                                  20   harms competition.” Opp. 14. WFG argues that GFI fails to meet the pleading standard because

                                  21   the SAC lacks facts suggesting harm to “competition” in the broad sense of the word. Mot. 10.

                                  22   The Supreme Court of California has stated that “any finding of unfairness to competitors under

                                  23   [the UCL] must be tethered to some legislatively declared policy or proof of some actual or

                                  24   threatened impact on competition.” Cel-Tech, 20 Cal. 4th at 186. And claims resulting from “a

                                  25   direct competitor’s ‘unfair’ act or practice” requires “conduct that threatens an incipient violation

                                  26   of an antitrust law, or violates the policy or spirit of one of those laws because its effects are

                                  27   comparable to or the same as a violation of the law, or otherwise significantly threatens or harms

                                  28   Case No.: 24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO DISMISS
                                                                                           6
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD           Document 141         Filed 11/04/24      Page 7 of 9




                                   1   competition.” Id. The “antitrust laws’ prohibitions focus on protecting the competitive process

                                   2   and not on the success or failure of individual competitors.” Cascade Health Sols. v.

                                   3   PeaceHealth, 515 F.3d 883, 902 (9th Cir. 2008).

                                   4          While Plaintiffs’ primary theory is that WFG’s actions have chilled, and continues to chill,

                                   5   competition to GFI (see SAC 7 (Mrs. Olson “created GFI to compete with WFG, but she has been

                                   6   impeded by WFG’s Restrictive Covenant and WFG’s lawsuit against her”)), the SAC also alleges

                                   7   injury to competition more broadly. See SAC ¶¶ 42 (contract provisions “chill[] any lay person

                                   8   reading it from engaging in legitimate competition”), 48 (inclusion of the Restrictive Covenant

                                   9   “has chilled competition by limiting mobility among WFG’s current and former agents in

                                  10   California”). But, again, allegations based on the Restrictive Covenant in agent agreements cannot

                                  11   form the basis of the UCL claim because GFI is not a party to those agreements. GFI also refers

                                  12   to (without citing any specific allegations in the SAC) WFG’s alleged actions in stealing
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   confidential information and terminating employees. Those allegations appear to relate solely to

                                  14   GFI’s harm and not harm to competition more broadly. See SAC ¶¶ 57 (“WFG has on multiple

                                  15   occasions threatened to terminate (and in many cases terminated) the spouse of any agent that

                                  16   moves to GFI”); 78 (“WFG obtained non-public information about GFI’s provider relationships

                                  17   for purposes of interfering with those relationships”). Unlike the complaint in Diva Limousine, a

                                  18   case GFI relies on, the SAC here has not alleged conduct by WFG that “violates the policy or

                                  19   spirit of [an antitrust] law[] because its effects are comparable to or the same as a violation of the

                                  20   law, or otherwise significantly threatens or harms competition.” Diva Limousine, 392 F. Supp. 3d

                                  21   at 1091 (UCL claim sufficiently plead where plaintiff “alleged that Uber’s misclassification of

                                  22   drivers allows it to shirk its legal obligations under the California Labor Code and Wage Orders

                                  23   issued by the California Industrial Welfare Commission to provide adequate pay and benefits to its

                                  24   drivers”).

                                  25          Accordingly, the Court grants WFG’s motion to dismiss GFI’s claim under the “unlawful”

                                  26   and “unfair” prong of the UCL.

                                  27

                                  28   Case No.: 24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO DISMISS
                                                                                          7
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD           Document 141         Filed 11/04/24     Page 8 of 9




                                   1          B.       Tortious Interference with Contract

                                   2          GFI alleges that WFG tortiously interfered with GFI’s insurance provider contracts,

                                   3   including by inducing Mr. Perez to access Mr. Olson’s emails. SAC ¶¶ 78, 80–82. WFG

                                   4   contends GFI’s tortious interference with contract claim fails for three reasons: (1) WFG cannot be

                                   5   held liable for torts committed by its independent contractors, (2) GFI has not alleged any

                                   6   independently wrongful conduct, and (3) GFI has not established WFG’s actual knowledge of the

                                   7   contracts before they were terminated.

                                   8          Tortious interference with contract requires “(1) the existence of a valid contract between

                                   9   the plaintiff and a third party; (2) the defendant’s knowledge of that contract; (3) the defendant’s

                                  10   intentional acts designed to induce a breach or disruption of the contractual relationship; (4) actual

                                  11   breach or disruption of the contractual relationship; and (5) resulting damage.” Ixchel Pharma,

                                  12   LLC v. Biogen, Inc., 9 Cal. 5th 1130, 1141 (2020).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          GFI alleges interference with at-will insurance provider contracts. Mot. 13; see also Opp.

                                  14   2 (not disputing the relevant contracts are at-will). To assert a claim for interference with an at-

                                  15   will contract, “the plaintiff must allege that the defendant engaged in an independently wrongful

                                  16   act.” Ixchel, 9 Cal. 1130 at 1148. “[A]n act is independently wrongful if it is unlawful, that is, if

                                  17   it is proscribed by some constitutional, statutory, regulatory, common law, or other determinable

                                  18   legal standard.” Id. at 1142 (quoting Korea Supply Co. v. Lockheed Martin Corp., 29 Cal. 4th

                                  19   1134 (2003)).

                                  20          WFG argues GFI’s tortious interference claim fails because GFI has not alleged any

                                  21   independently wrongful act. Mot. 13. GFI responds that it has alleged WFG “ask[ed]” Mr. Perez

                                  22   to obtain confidential information from email accounts from the Olsons. Opp. 6 (citing SAC

                                  23   ¶ 78). As above, GFI has not explained which constitutional, statutory, regulatory, common law,

                                  24   or other legal standard WFG violated by instructing Mr. Perez to obtain confidential information

                                  25   from the Olsons. Cf. Korea Supply, 29 Cal. 4th at 1159 (plaintiff satisfied the independent

                                  26   wrongfulness requirement by alleging defendant engaged in bribery and offered sexual favors in

                                  27   violation of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act). Should GFI amend its complaint to state why this

                                  28   Case No.: 24-cv-00477-EJD
                                       ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO DISMISS
                                                                                          8
                                         Case 5:24-cv-00477-EJD            Document 141          Filed 11/04/24   Page 9 of 9




                                   1   conduct is unlawful, the Court can better assess whether GFI has sufficiently alleged the wrongful

                                   2   act required to state its tortious interference claim.

                                   3           Because GFI has failed to sufficiently allege an independently wrongful act, its tortious

                                   4   interference with contract claim fails, and the Court need not reach WFG’s remaining arguments.

                                   5   However, the Court observes that GFI appears to have sufficiently alleged WFG had knowledge of

                                   6   the contractual relationships between GFI and NLG, Athene, and F&G. See SAC ¶¶ 79 (“WFG

                                   7   has been tracking and monitoring contracts with insurance providers and communicating with

                                   8   insurance providers”), 129 (“Defendants knew of the existence of those contracts and/or

                                   9   contractual relationships between GFI and NLG, Athene, F&G and other providers”). The Court

                                  10   also rejects WFG’s argument that it cannot be held liable for torts committed by its independent

                                  11   contractors because GFI has “alleg[ed] facts from which an inference can be drawn that [WFG]

                                  12   had the power to control the general” conduct of its agents and executives. Hellum v. Breyer, 194
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Cal. App. 4th 1300, 1317 (2011) (quotations omitted); see e.g., SAC ¶¶ 78 (“WFG obtained non-

                                  14   public information about GFI’s provider relationships for purposes of interfering with those

                                  15   relationships”), 130 (WFG “induced a disruption or breach of the contractual relationship” by

                                  16   “pressuring insurance providers to cancel GFI’s contracts”).

                                  17   IV.     CONCLUSION
                                  18           For the reasons stated above, WFG’s motion to dismiss GFI’s claims is GRANTED.

                                  19   Because the deficiencies can be cured, and GFI has not had an opportunity to amend its tortious

                                  20   interference claim, GFI is permitted leave to amend. Any amended complaint must be filed within

                                  21   21 days of this order. Should GFI amend the deficiencies identified in this order, the Court

                                  22   expects GFI’s claims may proceed. The Court encourages the parties to confer to avoid the need

                                  23   for further motion practice regarding any amended complaint.

                                  24           IT IS SO ORDERED.
